kosala.t: The 16 dreams of King Pasenadi of Kosala
kosala.b: From the Jataka tales: sixteen ancient dreams and the original text's predictions about a declining age, retold as historical literature.
Four black bulls get ready to fight, then back away. — Rain clouds will gather from four directions and thunder, yet drift away without rain.
Saplings barely out of the ground flower and fruit. — People will marry before they are of age.

kosala.t: A mother cow suckling from a calf
kosala.b: A grown cow drinks milk from a newborn calf. — Parents will have to depend on their children's earnings.

kosala.t: Young bulls yoked to heavy carts
kosala.b: Strong bulls are set aside and untrained young ones yoked; they collapse. — The inexperienced will be given high office and government will fall into disorder.
A horse eats with two mouths and is never full. — Some judges will take bribes from both sides.

kosala.t: A gold bowl given to an old dog
kosala.b: A priceless gold bowl is given to an old dog and misused. — The old text says those of noble birth will marry unsuitable partners for money.
As a man plaits a rope, a jackal eats it from behind. — The old text says some will squander what their spouse has earned.

kosala.t: Filling only the big full pot
kosala.b: Water is poured into an overflowing big pot while the empty small ones are ignored. — Heavy taxes will be taken from the poor to make the rich richer.

kosala.t: A pond muddy in the middle, clear at the edge
kosala.b: A lotus pond is muddy in the centre and clear by the banks. — Cities will be burdened with taxes and people will live better in the countryside.

kosala.t: Rice cooked unevenly in one pot
kosala.b: Rice in one pot is raw in places, mushy in others, and done elsewhere. — Rulers will be unjust and rain will fall unevenly.
Precious sandalwood is traded for cheap sour gruel. — Some monks will use the Teaching for money.
Light dry gourds that should float sink under the water. — The words of the wise and good will be ignored.
Great boulders float on the water like wood. — The unworthy will rise to fame and honour.
Tiny frogs swallow deadly cobras. — The old text says older spouses will be bullied by much younger partners.
Golden geese bow and serve a black crow. — The wise and virtuous will have to bow to bad rulers.
Lions, tigers and leopards run from goats in fear. — The wicked will hold power and good people will have to hide.

title.disclaimer: Compiled from traditional Myanmar dream texts and rewritten. Shown as cultural knowledge only; not a prediction or medical or financial advice.

intro.p1: Everyone dreams. In traditional Myanmar belief, some dreams are omens of good or bad things to come, while dreams caused by an imbalance of the body's elements are not taken as omens.
intro.p2: When a dream seemed to be an omen, earlier generations asked someone skilled in reading dreams or consulted dream texts. A good omen was awaited mindfully; a bad one was eased by paying respect to the Triple Gem, parents and teachers, by doing good deeds and by traditional remedies (yadaya).
intro.p3: Tradition says that bad dreams come when unwholesome karma is about to bear fruit, and good dreams when wholesome karma is. The old texts often disagree, so please read this dictionary as cultural knowledge.

remedy.1: Whether good or bad, a dream is traditionally told in the morning to someone who understands dreams.
remedy.2: After a good dream, people offer a lamp to the Buddha, tell the dream and wish for long life, honour and plenty. Some first pay respect to their teachers.
remedy.3: After a bad dream, some place a handful of rice and a cup of water on a tree stump, eat something tasty, and only then tell the dream.
remedy.4: Other customs: washing the hair with blessed paritta water, offering water, umbrellas, banners and flowers at a pagoda, and propping up a Bodhi tree.
remedy.5: According to the hermit Ankura's text, paying respect to the Triple Gem, parents and teachers and keeping the uposatha precepts turns bad fortune into good.
remedy.6: A Myanmar saying holds that a good remedy can avert even great misfortune. Customs include washing the hair with eight medicinal herbs and offering flowers at a pagoda, one for each year of one's age.
